paragraphs.text: Come today as well, O blessed Paul. Leave behind the overly subtle arguments of the Stoics and, by the wisdom of the Spirit, as a spiritual man comparing spiritual things with spiritual, seal in us too the word of the cross, which you faithfully sealed for the Corinthians when you said: “The word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” The divine grace of the cross, proclaimed through Paul, has brought light to the whole world. Did the Lord lie, brothers, when he said of him to Ananias, “This man is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before the Gentiles”? By the grace of the cross of Christ this Paul silenced the noise of the orators and exposed the myths of the poets, saying somewhere, “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” He also pulled down the conceit of the philosophers and the sacred precincts of the temples, saying, “If anyone thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, so that he may become wise.” “For the foolishness of God,” he says, “is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.” He showed everyone the disappearance of the idols and the overthrow of the oracles, the flight of the demons and the lament of the devil, the death of death and the emptying of the tombs, the resurrection of the dead and the steadfastness of the martyrs, the contests of the athletes and the speed of the runners, the valour of the soldiers and the prizes of the crowns. In all of these, brothers, he rightly sang the praises of the power of the cross, saying: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of Christ.” Now you, O blessed Paul, have fought the good fight well and have won the crown; but the children of the Greeks and the Jews still sit beside the word of the cross and laugh. They do not grasp the greatness of the proclamation, but see only the shame of the cross, and they bring this up as an insult and say, “We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” So arm our soul, forge our mind, sharpen our tongue, give sinew to our thinking, make our voice run freely, and work with us in everything like a good president of the games. Obtain for us strength of speech from God the Word, who said through the Gospel, “Do not worry about what you will say, for a word will be given to you,” so that, having strengthened the word of truth by our words, we may refute the irrational and shameless counsel of the Greeks and the Jews—that counsel which God also rejected through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “I will turn the wise back and make their counsel foolish.”

Let the cross come into our midst today, the cross that conquered Egypt: Egypt mad for idols, Egypt unclean and at war with God. So many God-sent plagues came upon her in the time of Moses, beloved, and yet she did not repent, shameless and blasphemous as she was, but cried out, “I do not know the Lord.” Do you see a brazen and shameless face? Let the prophet Jeremiah speak of the synagogue that behaved as she did, or rather to all who hold fast to dark impiety: “You had the face of a harlot; you were shameless toward all.” Do you see that lawless, profane Egyptian people behaving shamelessly in the face of God's great wonders and saying, “I do not know the Lord”? But at that time the Egyptians were disobedient and refused to listen. Today, however, beloved, after the Saviour's coming, after the cross and the death he accepted for our sake, after his resurrection from the dead and his ascent into heaven, though so many punishments have befallen the Egyptians and still befall them, they do not deny the cross—or rather, they do not deny the crucified Christ. Together with the whole world they worship the Lord whom they did not know when they blasphemed him; they worship him whom they formerly denied; they praise the Lord who brought the Israelite people out of their land with a mighty hand and an uplifted arm. They praise him who struck Egypt with ten plagues. O new and astonishing wonder! In the time of Moses the Egyptians, though scourged—or rather, to tell the truth, put to death—did not believe in God, but cried out with shameless mouth, “I do not know the Lord.” Yet today, after the cross of the Only-Begotten, they confess the sins they formerly committed; they give thanks, as David bears witness, to him “who did great wonders in Egypt, in the land of Ham, fearful things at the Red Sea”; and they sing that song which Moses taught the people in the wilderness against them, saying, “This is my God, and I will glorify him.” Do you see the grace of the cross? Do you see the power of the Crucified? Do you see how, after the cross, the Egyptians glorify the God whom they once denied, and say, “This is my God, and I will glorify him”?

O the indescribable grace of the Only-Begotten! O the unspeakable love for humankind of God the Word! For he who was God before the ages consented to become a man for our sake. He consented to become a man in order to make human beings truly human, to make human beings of the Egyptians—or rather of all those who were once irrational and lived the life of nomads. For though they were fashioned in honour, they lived in dishonour, as blessed David bears witness when he says, “Man, being in honour, did not understand.” Since, then, they lived in dishonour, the Lord accepted being struck by men on the cross, so that the devil might no longer strike us; he accepted being struck in order to heal our wounds. And it is not I who say this; Isaiah bears witness: “By his wound we were healed.” Christ was spat upon. He who by spitting healed the man blind from birth was spat upon; the face brighter than the sun was spat upon. For this sun is a thing of the senses, but Christ is proclaimed by the prophets as the Sun of righteousness. It is not I who say it; Malachi bears witness about him: “For you who fear the Lord,” he says, “the Sun of righteousness will rise, with healing in his wings.” Christ was spat upon in the face so that Isaiah might be proved true when he said, “He did not turn his face away from the shame of spitting.” The Lover of humankind died for us as a man, in order to kill the death of humankind, so that all of us may boast with Paul and say: “O death, where is your sting? O Hades, where is your victory?”

I am not ashamed of the cross, dearly beloved brothers, for I was dead because of sin, and through it I have come back to life. I do not blush at the Lord's passion, for through it I have risen from the depths of Hades; and indeed, praying to the Lord himself, I sing with the prophet and say, “Lord, you have brought my soul up from Hades.” Through the cross I have become a citizen of heaven, and from the regions under the earth I have flown up to the heavens. Paul bears witness to this too, when he says, “Our citizenship is in heaven.” The Life of all flesh was handed over to death, so that he might free everyone from the death that Adam brought upon us. Jesus, who gives food to all flesh, was hungry, in order to heal the sin that came through Adam's eating. And what kind of food Christ received from the Jews in its place you have heard him say through the prophet: “And they gave me gall for my food.” Again, he who brought water like rivers out of the rock was thirsty. He who gave drink to the ungrateful people in the wilderness was thirsty. He who provided the Jews with water from the flinty rock was thirsty, as Paul bears witness: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” He was thirsty—and what drink they gave him to cure his thirst, hear David tell: “And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” He who hung the heaven without supports [?] was hung on the cross. He who covers the firmament with clouds was stripped of his garments. He who established the earth upon the waters was hung on the cross, and he who judges every living thing was condemned to death. And that he is the judge of all, hear him say through the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son.” The Lord was bound on the cross—he who sets free those fettered in the prison house, who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. Jesus was bound—he who set free Lazarus, bound in the bonds of death. Jesus, the Christ and God who is before the ages, was judged by men; the King of glory was judged by Pilate; he was judged by a governor and kept silent, so that Isaiah might be proved true when he said, “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and when he was judged he did not open his mouth.”

In this way the Jews were put to shame; in this way the devil, thinking he was killing, was himself killed. The Lord set up a trophy against him: he set up the cross, and by it he put him to death. Foreseeing this wood, the prophet cried out, “You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water. You shattered the head of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.” For from that time on even children play upon his head, since Jesus pulled down his dominion through the cross. They clothed the Lord—in purple, as John the evangelist says; in a scarlet cloak, as Matthew and Mark say—and they put a crown of thorns on his head and a reed in his right hand. And kneeling down they worshipped him, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews!” Truly a very great wonder and an astonishing thing, a sign of Christ's victory and a token of his great grace. Hear how. The one they had condemned to death as a man, they unwillingly worshipped as God; the one they despised as worthless, they called king; the one they stripped of his garments in mockery, they clothed in purple; the one they denied knowing, they addressed as a prophet, saying, “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” And to the one they mocked and struck with a reed, they handed the tokens of victory: they clothed him in a scarlet cloak, put a crown of thorns on his head, and a reed in his right hand.

You, then, lawless Jews, dare to do such things against Christ, but he, through the very things you do, despoils the devil. “For the earth, through sin, was being defiled with murder by the enemy, and was filled with human blood more than with water. First it received the blood of righteous Abel, and from then on men went on mingling blood with blood, as the prophet also says: ‘Cursing and lying and murder and theft and adultery are poured out upon the earth, and they mingle blood with blood.’ And for this reason the earth had become accursed, for God said to Cain, ‘Cursed is the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.’ And even before this it had been rebuked because of Adam's disobedience and condemned to bring forth thorns and thistles. Since, then, the earth was filled with blood and thorns, and the chorus of the prophets, grieving over the earth's condemnation, cried out, ‘I was turned to misery while a thorn was fixed in me,’ Jesus, on his way to the cross, consented to bear these things, in order through them to revoke the curse on the earth. For before the cross and the Lord's passion the enemy held sway over all, and the tyrant, holding the bond of our sins that stood against us, was greatly puffed up. But once Christ had borne this on the cross, it was from then on made void. The blood that had polluted the earth he took up in the scarlet cloak, its thorns in the crown, and the bond that stood against us in the reed—for with this the devil had long been writing down our sins—so that our Saviour and God might blot these out together with death through the cross, and, having cleansed the whole creation, might grant us, in place of the thorns of the curse, the tree of life, the cross; and in place of the blood of sin, his own holy and gracious blood, of which David said, ‘Taste and see that the Lord is gracious.’

O how great are the things done for us! Christ poured out his own blood upon the earth, and at once wiped away the blood of sin. Christ emptied out his blood upon the earth, and in place of thistles and thorns, through his three-day burial, life and immortality dawned for the world—the life made manifest to us through faith. Of this David too cried out, saying, ‘I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.’ Jesus wore a crown of thorns in order to take away our anxiety and not allow the deceitfulness of life to choke the divine seed he has sown in us, but to make it bear fruit, as he himself promised, in some thirtyfold, in others sixtyfold, and in others a hundredfold. Again, the Lord received a reed in his right hand against the devil himself. How? I will tell you. The reed is a killer of snakes; we know that they are killed with it more readily than with anything else. Taking this reed, then, Jesus made war on the great and deadly serpent—the one of whom Isaiah said, ‘The Lord will bring his holy sword against the dragon, against the crooked serpent,’ the great devil. So Jesus Christ pursued the devil holding the reed in his hand, the weapon that kills the great beast; for with this reed he dealt the devil a mortal blow. And just as David once did to Goliath—after striking him on the forehead with the stone, he ran, took Goliath's own sword, cut off his head, and carrying it, sang, ‘The sinner is caught in the works of his own hands’—so too the Saviour did on the cross: taking the reed in his hand from the Jews, the sons of the devil, with it he put the devil to death.” That those who do the devil's works are sons of the devil, the Lord bears witness when he says to the Jews, “You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the works of your father.”

But let us return to our subject. After the tyrant had fallen this great fall and the word of the Lord had been fulfilled which says, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven,” then at last the Jews laid the cross upon the Lord, thereby making it the greatest token of his victory. For as long as the devil stood, the crowds held the wood; but when he received the mortal blow and fell, then at last Christ was shown to be the victor, and taking the trophy for himself, he carried the cross. For it was fitting—truly fitting—that he who was to conquer the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, should himself carry the trophy against the enemy, and on it lead him and the wicked demons in triumph. According to John, brothers, Christ carried the cross himself, but according to Matthew and the other evangelists, Simon of Cyrene carried it. Yet this does not contradict them—far from it, for the apostles do not write things that contradict one another—but both happened: the Saviour carried the cross himself, and then Simon carried it as well. And there is a spiritual meaning in this too. Christ carried the cross as a trophy against the devil, to show that he came to the cross willingly and not under compulsion. And Simon also carried it, to show everyone that he was crucified not for his own sake but for us human beings and for our salvation.

For the Lord did everything for our sake. For example: Christ consented to be stripped of his garments in order to clothe us in the garment of incorruption, of which Paul says, “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” Again, he wore a seamless tunic, woven from the top throughout, so that through this too we might believe who it was that wore it and where he had come from. For God the Word came to us not from below but from above. This tunic, then, the soldiers did not dare to divide. Why? To show that the great only-begotten Word and Son is undivided from the great Father. The other garments, however, they divided into four parts, casting lots, so that the prophecy of David might be fulfilled, which says, “They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots”; and so that, while showing everyone that the Lord was accomplishing salvation for the whole fourfold world, the Saviour's seamless tunic remained undivided. Let the Arians and Eunomians, who divide the Son from the Father's essence, hear that the soldiers did not dare to divide the Saviour's tunic—that is, the incarnation of the Godhead. Yet these people divide, calling one great and one lesser, and the Spirit lesser still than the lesser, even though they hear Christ say, “I and the Father are one.” And again, concerning the Spirit, Paul cries out, “Now the Lord is the Spirit.” The Saviour's tunic, it says, was seamless—that is, Christ's body was not stitched together from a man and a woman, but came from a virgin alone, woven by the craft of the Holy Spirit, as the angel bears witness when he says to the Virgin, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

This being so, beloved, he then comes to the place called the Place of the Skull, carrying the cross himself. And going up onto the wood, he took the bond of our sins that stood against us out of the enemy's hands and nailed it to the cross, and tearing it with the nails, he made it void from then on. And having become obedient to death, as Paul says, even death on a cross, he thus prepared for us the way up to heaven. And the Truth himself, Jesus Christ, bears witness to my words when he says, “Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me.” For God the Word, though immortal, suffered in the flesh for our sake, so that we who die because of the devil who deceived us might rise together with the Lord in power, as Scripture says: “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” For this is why Christ took a body like ours: to clothe our perishable nature with incorruption and our mortal nature with immortality, so that we might no longer have death reigning over us, as Paul bears witness when he says, “Death no longer has dominion over you.” For by his own death Jesus, the Christ and God, put to death the death that was against us. To him be glory, might, honour and worship, with the Father and his all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
